utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I just have one preliminary question with your leave related to the OTP witness Ewa Tabeau. Namely yesterday OTP requested admission of uploading -- uploaded report which was filed just yesterday and which is conducted during the weekend which wasn't on the 65 ter list. They did not request admission of the basic report from 2001 which was filed on 65 ter list and I tried to compare those two reports and I found some discrepancies and actually for the preparation of cross-examination I need additional time because this is a completely new -- new matter. That is completely new report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, I know you weren't dealing with this, but are you in a position to respond?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, my understanding is and Ms. Marcus will actually be taking one of the witnesses this afternoon so she may be able to deal more specifically with it, but my understanding of this new report is it simply reflects -- none of the conclusions have changed. It simply reflects some new data that has become available recently and Ms. Tabeau just updated the data sources. But and Mr. Cepic to correct me if I'm wrong, but it's my understanding that none of her conclusions regarding the report have changed in any way. It's simply updating some of the numbers as reflected in some newly acquired data.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Cepic, if I understand you correctly then, you -- you have done a comparison between the new updated report and the old one of 2001 and you have found discrepancies.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Precisely, Your Honour. Actually, I couldn't do in very short period of time to complete my comparison, but as far as I understand up to now, there are different sources, there are some differences, some discrepancies, but for the -- to complete my comparison, I need additional time. That's the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That is the -- that's your basic problem. You say you need additional time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Because we were scheduled to have you on tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: For cross-examination. Now we have a witness on Thursday, and it is very important that we take that witness, as I understand it. Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I would be renewing my application to deal Thursday with a particular witness, start and finish that witness on a single day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But, Mr. Cepic, if you have this report and you're able to find discrepancies, why do you need more time if you've already found the discrepancies?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, yesterday is disclosed the new updated report, and I couldn't do that in just couple hours. As I said, I couldn't complete my -- my comparation between those two material, and additionally yesterday we received and the Prosecutor requested admission of two new tables which they contain the names of missing persons. This is also new material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, I see you have three more witnesses lined up for this week, on the 23rd, the 24th, and the 25th.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, one of those witnesses is a witness that we made an application for a subpoena. It's my understanding that it's kind of out of our hands now so we're not even sure when this witness -- if the witness receives the subpoena when they'll arrive in The Hague. I don't know whether that witness is here. Perhaps the court officer can inform the Chamber whether it's likely that VG-17 will appear this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The court officer doesn't have any information right now, but she's expecting some news shortly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, when Ms. Marcus arrives, and she has greater familiarity with this matter, I'll deal with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Is there any other procedural matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Well, let the witness be called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please sit. And, Dr. Clark, you remain subject to the declaration that you made. Ms. Mazzocco, you had completed your examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAZZOCCO
utterances.text: I suppose there should be the cross by the Defence counsel for Sredoje Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Dieckmann has prepared some questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Dieckmann. Mr. Dieckmann, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Dr. Clark, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: My name is Jens Dieckmann and I am counsel for Sredoje Lukic. Since your report that is P122 in evidence is not directly related to our client, I just have some questions for clarification.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Dr. Clark, when you conducted your autopsies did you have any indication as to when these people died?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Other than just the information we were given that they had died in about 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Did you have any indication as to how long they had been buried for?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Nothing specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Could the court officer call in evidence the document P122. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: I refer to the second paragraph, and I just would like to read the first sentences to make clear what I am referring to. I quote: "We were informed that these were alleged to be the bodies of people killed in or around Visegrad in the summer of 1992, including people who had been shot on the bridge and thrown over the side. Their bodies ended up in the River Drina below and were carried downstream for approximately 20 kilometres to where the river takes a major bend at Zepa. There, the bodies were recovered from the water by local people and buried in a wooded area a little distance away. They were placed into mainly individual graves, each marked by a wooden post on which a number or name was carved. At the time of the examination eight years later the site was designated as Slap 1." So, Dr. Clark, is it fair to say that prior to your involvement in these autopsies you have already received information that these bodies had been in the ground for circa eight years?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the general information, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: So there wasn't --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry --

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I suppose, yeah, it would be eight years. I was going to say that the information was that they were killed eight years earlier but I suppose by inference they were probably buried around about the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. So there was no independent assessment to contradict that assumption?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: So before you were involved in the specific autopsies, did you receive some briefing from an investigator involved with the ICTY or investigators of local authorities?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We received a briefing document from a local Judge, cantonal Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: So is it fair to say that you were informed in a general sense as to the perceived is circumstances under which these victims had met their deaths before you started the specific autopsy?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a general sense, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: I think I'm too fast. Yes. Okay. So you would not have come to the case with an open mind as to whether these were potentially victims in a combat situation as equally as victims in alleged execution. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think professionally I can -- I can maintain an independence. It's not difficult. And if I had come across evidence that these were combat casualties in the sense that we found military clothing or ammunitions, that would most certainly be recorded in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: In your mind the balance weighed in favour of the fact that these were people who had been victims of alleged executions. Is it correct to say, that there was rather a balance that they are victims?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, again in the sense that there was no real evidence that these were any military background here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. So again in fact you do not know how long the recovered bodies were buried there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not specifically, no. Not precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: And in fact -- in fact, you do not know if these bodies -- in fact, you do not know if these bodies have spent any time in water before being buried?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that specifically, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The changes on -- affecting a body being in a water are on the skin and other soft tissues, and of course that was present, so I can't specifically say they were in water.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: So due to your examinations -- I'm sorry, there's a translation problem with the B/C/S. I'm sorry. So if I may conclude. Due to your examination and your scope of examinations, it is equally likely that these bodies were never in the water of the Drina River?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: I don't have any further questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dieckmann. Any re-examination, Ms. Mazzocco?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAZZOCCO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAZZOCCO
utterances.text: Dr. Clark, did you find the personal possession on the bodies?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We found some personal possessions, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAZZOCCO
utterances.text: Did you find clothing on the bodies?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the majority of bodies, yes, were clothing.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAZZOCCO
utterances.text: Did you find any military clothing on the bodies?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please observe a pause for the benefit of the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAZZOCCO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I didn't hear that last question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAZZOCCO
utterances.text: Did you find any firearms or bullets in their possession -- or bullet, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. I don't think we found any firearms. I think on one of the bodies in Slap 2, we found three bullets.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAZZOCCO
utterances.text: Can be displayed page 7 of Exhibit P122.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I can see what you're getting at. I've specifically said that none of the victims was wearing any military clothing and none had any firearms or bullets in their possession. I would qualify that by, having looked at the files again that in the grave of one of the bodies in Slap 2, I do remember we found three bullets. Whether they belonged to that body or not I don't know, but they were in that grave.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAZZOCCO
utterances.text: Were these bullet in the clothing of this body or in the body itself?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, just loose in -- loose in -- these were unused. These were unused rounds of application which were in -- in the grave. Not necessarily with the body, but they were beside the body.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAZZOCCO
utterances.text: Thank you. And is it possible to say how long it takes for a body to became a skeleton?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends entirely where the body is. A body will degenerate to a skeleton -- if it's left outside in the air, depending on the time of year, depending on whether there are animals and insects about, a body could be reduced to a skeleton as quickly as six or seven weeks or so, but equally long -- it could be much longer. A body that is in water will take longer to decompose or to reduce to skeleton, and a body that is buried will take even longer. It's an impossible question to answer, I'm afraid. I have seen people -- bodies reduced to a skeleton within eight weeks -- six weeks, six weeks in fact, yet many of the bodies that we saw in other grave sites in my work in the Balkans had been buried for equal amount of time and still had a lot of flesh on them. It is very variable.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAZZOCCO
utterances.text: Thank you. Was there -- was there any judicial authority present at the time of exhumation?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that certainly in the Slap -- Slap 2 cases --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, just in interest to speed up procedure. I think we already have this answer, and some questions sounds to me that this is a new direct examination. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How does this arise, Ms. Mazzocco?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAZZOCCO
utterances.text: Because yesterday in the cross-examination was suggested some mishandling of the bodies, that the bodies could be mixed up and not well brought to the mortuary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, very well. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAZZOCCO
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly on the exhumation of the Slap 2 bodies, because I was actually present at that time, there was a Judge. A local Judge was there. I do not know who was present in the Slap 1 bodies, but I can only imagine that there would have been a Judge there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAZZOCCO
utterances.text: And was there any judicial authority present at the time of identification?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there was, yes. I think the same Judge was present at least some of the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAZZOCCO
utterances.text: And going back to that identification of Osmanagic, that body 361, the Exhibit P124, can you explain where it happened?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The identification?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAZZOCCO
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: From memory we worked -- we worked in a mortuary in Visoko, and this was -- also happened to be the local graveyard and undertaker, so we handed the bodies back to them in the same area, and the identification subsequently took place actually on the roof of our mortuary.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAZZOCCO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAZZOCCO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Doctor. That concludes your evidence. We thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And you're now dismissed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The next witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next Prosecution witness is Mirsad Tokaca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by your leave just for the transcript, we do not see the testimony of this witness as relevant because he is not an eyewitness in terms of the indictment with regard to this legal matter, or he is a hearsay witness, if I can put it that way. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't understand why you say that, because we take in hearsay evidence in this judicial system.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, while we're waiting for the witness there's one matter I would like to ask the Chamber to give some consideration to. With a view towards expediting the witnesses that the Prosecution has -- has a pending application to -- to add to our witness list, I would note that today we have provided unredacted statements of all the witnesses to Defence counsel not in anticipation of the Chamber's decision but at least give them the most notice about the statements. With one exception and that one where we're seeking a particular protective measure in terms of redaction of one of the statements. My question to the Chamber is -- or what I would ask the Chamber to consider is we have not had an opportunity to explore with any of these people whether there's a need for protective measures, and I'm wondering whether -- what the views of Defence counsel would be and whether the Chamber would consider if we dealt with the issue of protective measures on an oral basis so that when the witness arrives we can bring to the Chamber's attention any concern they have and a decision could be made or would the Chamber require us to do the standard written filings for protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have not receive any material related to some witnesses, and my learned friend Mr. Groome can remind me, Professor Markovic, I haven't found his name on the list. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It may be in transit now, but I issued a directive this morning that they be disclosed today. So it may be just at the end of the day now that they're received. If there's any problem I would be happy to deal -- discuss that with Defence counsel after court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting, but who is Professor Markovic? I never heard before that name on the list of witnesses. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Nor have I, Your Honour. We discuss it after court. It may be perhaps this statement mentions a witness and it may be disclosed pursuant to Rule 68, but I would be happy to go over any of the statements with Mr. Cepic over the break or afterwards and clarify anything that's not clear from the statement itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: There's no problem with your raising the issue of protective measures orally.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. While we're on the matter of protective measures, I have spoken once again to Zehra Turjacanin to confirm that it really is indeed her wish to testify publicly and she reaffirmed to me earlier today that it is her wish not to have any protective measures so at this time I would be formally requesting that the protective measures pertaining to her be amended so that she testifies publicly in open session without the use of a pseudonym.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That is to be done. The witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit. And you may begin, Madam Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Friedman.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, will you please state your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: Mirsad Tokaca, born in Sarajevo on the 28th of July, 1954.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And, Your Honours, we'll be seeking to admit three video clips this afternoon through this witness and I'm conscious of the time limit for 92 ter witnesses. This witness has testified in three trials previously before this Tribunal. His educational and professional background and the work of his organisation is discussed in those trials, and I wanted to make an application to lead him through this information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Tokaca, I'm going to summarise your educational and professional background and I will ask you at the end if I have done so accurately. You studied in the University of Sarajevo where you received a diploma in political sciences and also studied law and economics. Before the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, you first worked as a journalist, later as an analyst of social policy and social welfare, and finally in financial marketing management and trade. At the start of the war you began to work for the state commission on gathering facts on war crimes in Bosnia-Herzegovina. This organisation was established in April 1992, and you began in the first months of this existence to volunteer your time. You were then asked to become secretary of the commission, which essentially means that you directed it, at August of 1992. Have I stated that accurately?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: Yes. Everything is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Next I will briefly summarise the activities of the commission and will ask you again at the end if it's accurate. The state commission on gathering facts on war crimes set out to gather all possible information about war crimes committed against all ethnicities using written statements, audiotapes, videotapes, and whatever was available. This work was undertaken in Sarajevo as well as in the field wherever additional premises could be established. All of the evidence was brought back to the central office in Sarajevo where it was organised, analysed, and archived. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Okay. And finally, I will just ask about your professional activities after you worked at the state commission. In 2003, you formed the Research and Documentation Centre, and you are the president of that institution. The Research and Documentation Centre functions independently of the government. It is engaged in various projects, including the human losses project and the Bosnian book of the dead. Have I stated that correctly?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Tokaca, what happened to the archives of the state commission?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: Well, you see, we faced many problems over a long period of time. There was pressure and we didn't have sufficient funds for the state commission, the work of the state commission, and after the peace agreement was signed bodies of government were joined by people who unfortunately were deeply involved in crimes against humanity. One of them, Mr. Krajisnik, was tried and convicted by this Tribunal not such a long ago which in practical terms made our work very difficult, if not impossible. I resigned in 2003 simply because we didn't have sufficient funds to continue our work and then I set up an institute, or, rather, it was a centre for research which dealt with researching war crimes. In a way I wanted a long-term commitment for myself in this line of work and I wanted to start what we -- I wanted to continue what we first started out doing as part of the state commission. All of these documents because at one point unfortunately the state started -- stopped keeping track of these documents, remained in the possession of the research institute. Therefore we physically in every way --

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: I think you're speaking a bit faster than me. Could you go a bit slower, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. I'm so sorry. Okay. I'm so sorry. I will try to respect.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, all of the documentation in our possession that we had collected over more than ten years is fully preserved are still available. We continue to comply with the requests made by any organs of the judiciary that had any interest in this documentation, which included this Tribunal and which at this point in time and over the coming years will probably also include the work of our special commission for war crimes, a special council for war crimes that was established in Sarajevo and has been active over the last three years.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. So the archives of the state commission on gathering facts on war crimes in Bosnia-Herzegovina, where are they now located?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: They're in the archive of the Research and Documentation Centre based in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Tokaca, do you recall testifying in the Vasiljevic trial on September 21st, 2001?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that well. It was about identifying certain video clips that were in our possession at the time. Yes, yes, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Have you had a chance to read that testimony in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And I know you are speaking today in B/C/S, but just for the record, were you able to understand that testimony in English?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: Yes. I understand English fully. I actually speak English but the circumstances being what they are, I'd not wish to leave any room for misinterpretation or anything of that nature, anything that is not fully in line with the extent to which I am a master of my mother tongue, but I have a full understanding of everything that is said and written in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And was your testimony accurate?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: If we asked you the same questions today would you give the same answers?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: I don't know if the wording would be the same but the essence would certainly remain the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution moves to tender 65 ter Exhibit 56, which is Mr. Tokaca's Vasiljevic testimony, into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P127, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: I would ask the court usher to switch to Sanction. It's not yet done. And if Mr. Van Hooydonk could call up 65 ter 193.1 but not play it yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Tokaca, do you see the first video -- the first still from this video in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: I have the image, but it's frozen.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell if this is a video that you've had a chance to see since coming to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And what is it?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: This is one of the refugee collection centres. I don't know the exact location, but I suppose it might have been somewhere in the surroundings of Zenica. I'm not entirely certain, though. Quite obviously, though, this is a refugee collection centre, a place where refugees were being put up at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Did the Research and Documentation Centre provide this video to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: Yes. There was a request from the OTP, and we secured the clip for you. It's in your hands now.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And how did you get this video originally?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: Well, you see, that would require me to explain our modus operandi at least in the roughest of terms. We tried to comply with certain standards when collecting facts, gathering facts about crimes that were committed in Bosnia-Herzegovina. We put together a methodology of work that was quite exhaustive and comprehensive which also entailed instructions on how such work would be performed. Of course, when we talk about methodology the question that always arises is the implementation stage unless of course you have all the right conditions in place for implementing that type of methodology, unless you have on the ground, you have all the manpower that you need for performing those tasks and if you're not able to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You are speaking too fast. The interpreter is having difficulty keeping up to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. [Interpretation] So you can create an ideal method, an ideal methodology, but if you don't have the people on the ground who are able to implement whatever methodology you come up with, then it's very difficult to secure very high standards to make sure you have high standards for gathering documents. Therefore, wherever we could, wherever we had a chance to implement this methodology we did so in the strictest of terms. On the other hand, you must know one thing. We worked under very difficult conditions. The commission was based in Sarajevo. Sarajevo was entirely encircled. And we used any form of communication open to us at the time to get in touch with people on the ground and in order to instruct them in the following way. If you can't use the methodology we selected -- I'm not just talking about professionals and I'm not just talking about volunteers. I'm talking about any citizen who happened to be in possession of any sort of photograph, video clip or anything like that or rather who had the equipment to record anything should try to take advantage of that technology or the equipment in their possession in order to record anything they could that was happening at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Can we go briefly into private session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] MV3: Crni Vrh and the other places around Visegrad. They chased us out by using poison. They drove them to these mountain areas, and in a refugee centre there are about 2.000 refugees taking refuge in the mountains, forests, and rocky ground. This is the first group that arrived, and we are expecting the arrival of other groups which are on their way. What people are saying, the village of Barimo sounds like a pure disaster. According to preliminary reports from the field there are 27 innocent victims, women, children and elderly people and all those who didn't manage to escape. They used rubber boats and the Chetniks crossed over to the left side of the Drina River. "MV4: This is the first time being photographed. "MV6: Hello, how is it going? Where is your father? "MV11: No, we are -- we went to Crni Vrh. "MV12: A pack of cigarettes, cameraman, what do you say? "MV11: Well, we started up 10.30. Now it's noon, so around 1300 or 1400 hours."

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: We have one more clip to show from this video, and that one I would ask to be not broadcast publicly. So if we could go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Tokaca, do you see this first still of the video on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Have you had a chance to view it since coming to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And what is in this video, just briefly?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: This is a map of Bosnia and Herzegovina focusing on the Visegrad area. As far as I remember, this was some TV coverage from Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Did the Research and Documentation Centre provide this to the OTP?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And does it depict Visegrad at the time of the takeover?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: Yes. This is, if I remember correctly, as far as this coverage is concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I've heard a lot of leading questions up to now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Be careful about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Actually, we can -- could we just play the video at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Tokaca, can you tell me when this video clip was taken?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: I can't give you the exact date, but I know for certain this was in the second half of April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: We tender this as an exhibit, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is admitted as Exhibit P130, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is not related to my case, but I just would like to raise that this video contains different two video clips from different -- from two different broadcasting company. One is Belgrade television and second is Sarajevo television, which is completely different, especially was different in that period of time, so ...

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: We can ask the witness about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, just a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, we don't wish to hear anything more about this. Have you then completed?

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Briefly, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Mr. Tokaca, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: My name is Jason Alarid and I represent Milan Lukic. I'd like to talk to you a little bit about your research and your background. Now, would it be fair to say that you were an activist brought to activism by the war?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, it was the -- it was the impetus of the war that changed your career path and you became an activist?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: The war changed my career path radically, if you like, but I was not an activist. This notion to me implies something altogether different. I'm not sure exactly what you mean when you use that term.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And I don't mean to imply that you were biased to one side or another. That's not what I'm coming at. What I'm more saying is that you -- you found a cause that you felt close to your heart and you went with that. That's not true?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: I simply don't quite understand what you're driving at.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, you established -- you established this organisation, correct, the commission for gathering of facts on war crimes?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: No, it wasn't me who established the commission. It was established by the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina by decision dated the 28th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And how much before the 28th of April, 1992, did you -- was the commission founded?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: No, no, no, no, no. It was founded on the 28th of April, 1992 by a decision of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. As of that moment, activities were commenced in establishing its work, setting up teams. There were teams that were at work. There was a political section comprising three members and the professional section and I was in charge of that section. Officially speaking, I was appointed on the 28th -- or, rather, the 18th of August, 1992. I was appointed secretary of the state commission. As of that moment, my role was to be technically in charge of all of the business of the state commission. That was one of the dimensions. This was about the professional section that comprised different professionals, historians, sociologists, and so on and so forth. On the other hand you had a three-member membership of the commission and Stjepan Kljujic was in charge of that. He was the president or the chairman of the commission, and then there was Mr. Miro Lazovic, who was there on behalf of the parliament and then there was Mr. Jahic, who was a minister in the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So roughly speaking this is how the commission was set up and this was by decision of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, then maybe just ask you out of your own mouth how did you gravitate towards the commission? Were you selected personally or did you apply for it out of your personal beliefs?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: At that point in time, May, June, July, I volunteered. It wasn't any sort of professional involvement and it was because I had certain experience in certain fields and had certain knowledge in certain fields. The people back at the Presidency and in the commission decided at the time that I was able to meet all the requirements for that appointment so this was not a public tender. This was something you got by appointment, and the only body with the power to make those appointments was the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But in -- but you put your name out there. You put your career out there to -- is that fair? And again, I'm not implying any kind of bias but I do want to sort of explore how in your heart you volunteered for this position. So what made you volunteer?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: I was fully dedicated, and this was a conscious decision and with an open mind. I had no dilemmas at the time, and I still don't. And this applies to the rest of my life as well as to the last 16 years of my life. I will continue to investigate any form of crime committed against the people of Bosnia and Herzegovina and then perhaps I could tell you about this too because this is more of a private angle on my part for all of this, my private reason. My entire family but rather my mother's family and my grandfather's family, my two uncles, their throats were slit back in 1942 during World War II, so in a way I had an intimate pre-war motive, a motive pre-dating the war in a way. So now you have this similar situation re-occurring as it were, and then I tried to record everything that was going on around me. I -- I tried to establish some sort of an historical record on what was going on in my country and this is something that you might call justice for all the innocent victims and also punishment for all those who actually committed the war crimes, so these were my private intimate motives that explain why I joined this project. I would never take it back, and I still believe in it as I believed in it on day one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. And I guess from reading some of the materials that I received from the Prosecution, it appears that your commission didn't care if it was a Muslim or a Serb or a Croat that was -- a crime was committed again, you would investigate all crimes. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. Not just the three principal ethnic groups but all the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That's what I'm telling you about. Of course I can't side who is who in terms of religion, ethnicity, social background, what their political background might be or some such. I was not politically involved. I was entirely independent and I worked in keeping with my own conscience, the dictate of my own conscience and in keeping with the rules, keeping perfectly in compliance with international criminal law and with all the rules established by international organisations in my work and I was adamant that this should be the same sort of position taken by all the people surrounding this project, there would be no discrimination of people along ethnic, religious or political lines. My entire work focused on that and I can even go as far as to say that at certain points in time I was subjected to certain forms of pressure and also certain attempts to get me to adopt that line of reasoning and to work in that way. I always resolutely refused to be part of that. It was never my conviction that this should be done and it never will be.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And I was looking at some of the data that we received, and it's my understanding that from some of your own research and documentation the centre revealed in 2007 that Serbs composed about approximately 25 per cent of the military deaths and 10 per cent of the civilian deaths in Bosnia. So there was some evidence of Serb casualties of course that your centre catalogued. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: Roughly speaking to the extent that I remember, the total, if you look at the population, 24.000 Serbs who became casualties of war as civilians -- or as civilians, as soldiers, over 10 per cent of that figure accounts for civilian casualties so, yes, we were collecting data on civilian casualties and of course also on military casualties, too, or, rather, soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And of course the collection of data was probably more difficult during the actual conflict and then you were probably able to rectify some of the numbers after things calmed down enough that you could collect data in a more efficient manner?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: Yes. It's always like that in wartime, isn't it, it's difficult to collect data. I was fully aware of the fact that errors could occur in wartime conditions. There was some forms of propaganda. So whatever I collected during the war, I tried to have another look to make sure everything was accurate. I looked at the losses, human losses in Bosnia and Herzegovina. We wanted to collect information on each and every citizen of Bosnia and Herzegovina who was killed during that period regardless of their affiliation to military units or along ethnic lines. I'm talking about the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: When -- and is it true that you incorporated some of the data from the 2004 report commissioned by the ICTY that -- that tried to calculate the casualties and the composition of casualties to as good a certainty as could be come to at the time? It's my understanding in the 2004 report that in the Bosnian conflict, military death toll was 58.3 per cent Muslim. Is that -- is that about right? 12.5 per cent Croatian, and 29.2 per cent Serbian, with the civilian death toll amongst the Serbian total being 30.5 per cent, and of course, I think that boils down to 10 per cent if you look at the total amount; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: Let me offer a dual answer to this. Our investigation was entirely independent and had nothing to do with the Tribunal's investigations. When we first -- first started preparing, I didn't even know that there were other people investigating. At a later point I found an article in a demographic journal by Ewa Tabeau, I think, and Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't get the name.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: -- and they publish the figures that you now refer to. We did not use the results of the Tribunal's work in our work. In terms of organisation, in terms of equipment and purely physical terms our investigation was entirely independent of the investigation pursued by the Tribunal but the results are more or less the same. I do have the information and there are some discrepancies between our results and the results that you now present, but ultimately the results are quite close.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And is -- is -- in being close, is it the difference between 102.000 people dead approximately and in 2007 the total was adjusted to 97.000 dead? Is that about right?

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Could we maybe see the report that counsel is referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: To be honest, I am referring to notes. I'm not referring to the actual report right now.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: It's just a little hard to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Let's see if the witness can answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you able to answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. You can get more or less the same results even if you applied to partially or entirely different methods. We used ours and they used theirs. There might be certain correlations but not necessarily. The difference between what we did on the one hand and what they did is this. We --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could all the other microphones please be switched off. The interpreters can't hear the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: Every time we published a figure there was always the identity of a specific victim behind it. We have the first name, the last name, and a number of other variables that we use for our research. Our research, our investigations included victims of direct war operations. So that was the figure that we arrived at, and that was our result. In addition to that kind of investigation, investigating direct victims of war, now we're working on the second pillar as it were, indirect victims of war, people who starved to death, for example, people who were victims of various accidents, for example, soldiers who ate some poisonous mushrooms, for example, some soldiers that were buried under an avalanche, so they weren't killed in an operation but for example --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to kindly slow down and repeat what he said. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The interpreter is asking you to slow down again. You're speaking too fast. Mr. Alarid, how much more time are you -- I would hope that we could conclude this witness's testimony by the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: When is our break, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: At a quarter to 4.00, because I have a suspicion that Mr. Cepic may not exert himself too much.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Precisely, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay. I'll do my best, Your Honour. I apologise. I'll do my best to speed things up.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But you're not allowed to speed things up because the interpreter can't keep up with you, so I'll just try and stay focused. Now you -- in your attempts to be objective, you even had Bosnian Serbs as experts on your commission. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But there was some things that came out. There was conflicting commission reports. Did you ever look at the Belgrade commission report of what happened in Visegrad? Even for the reading value, if not incorporating it to an analysis?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: We collected an enormous amount of reports, sources. We're looking at thousands of sources. I really don't remember specifically now, but I assume that we included whatever was available to us, be it from Belgrade, from Zagreb, from somewhere abroad.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could all the other microphones please be switched off. The interpreters can't hear the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. The interpreters again, a different concern this time, that the microphones are being left on, and that means that they can't hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Go ahead, sir.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: So, when I talk about human losses, and I understand that's what we're talking about, we included whatever we could, whatever was available to us regardless of the source. We calculated human losses based on thousands -- rather, hundreds of different sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And understanding that the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Understanding that the focus in Bosnia of course was of the displacement of the Muslim population, did you find instances of what could be classified as war crimes where Serbians were victims simply on an eye-for-an-eye situation even if it were sporadic?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: First of all, let me explain this. We didn't deal with the population movements. We dealt with murders, with expulsions and disappearances. When you classify crimes, you have to look at what the most serious crimes are, genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes. Of course, part of that problem is the expulsion of people from their homes. You saw the footage that was shown and then on the other hand we dealt with other forms of violence and war crimes which included, as I said, crimes against anyone, any ethnic group, Serbs, Bosniaks, Croats, or anyone else alike. We didn't discriminate along ethnic lines when it came to victims. I worked certain cases, by way of an example, Celebici where there were Serb victims, the camp at Celebici. There is a conviction to that effect. It's part of the case law before this Tribunal. I don't think this is the place to repeat this. You will see that all the other ethnicities were also part of our work. Our main principle was not to discriminate along ethnic lines when it came to victims. It was an ethical matter. It was a professional matter, and we always stuck to that. I was subjected to various attacks. I was subjected to criticism even back in Sarajevo, but I thought that the truth and the whole truth about the suffering of all those victims should be known and that was my top priority.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well -- and the reason I asked you that is I didn't see a statistic related to war crimes per se that we could apply to a Serb civilian population or something within the same war theatre of Bosnia because of course the whole country was embroiled in this conflict.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry if you didn't come across that, but I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Can you tell us what those data -- what those figures are from your memory?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: I cannot tell you figures from memory. I have brought with me an exhaustive report. I think the Tribunal has that at its disposal. A report on this. It's on this DVD here and all the data on all the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina, including those of Serbian ethnicity are here. This contains statistically very precise information by town, by municipality. If you're interested in names, for each of those locations we can find those names. For example, in the case of Visegrad, I have submitted this to the Prosecution also. You can find precisely how many citizens --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not going to allow you to pursue that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, what was interesting to me, and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: We attempted to uploaded it but I don't think it's up yet. Is it up? I'm not going to actually ask you to refer to things but I want to ask you some questions, is -- the commission for gathering facts on war crimes in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina put out a bulletin. Was that a monthly bulletin or was that a quarterly bulletin? What was it? And what I'm referring to personally is the March 1993 number 3 bulletin. I guess the first question is, you put out the bulletin; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: I was one of the people working on the bulletin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Because there's a series of essays or articles but I don't see individual authors for each essay, so I'm assuming that it was a group effort to put those articles together. Is that correct? Is that a yes?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: The members of the professional team, individual members, were authors of those texts. No one signed the texts. We discussed them beforehand, and we stood by those texts as the editorial board.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And of course these were -- these were journal articles that you had done some considerable research on before you published them. I mean, I'm assuming that you considered them good journalistic work or reporting work. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: More or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And the reason I say this is because this is really one of the first exposures that I've gotten to the war and how it began and it was very interesting to me to see that there was a concerted beginning of the war right around April of 1992 that happened in many regions of Bosnia and also in Croatia. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: The war did not begin in Bosnia at the same time it began in Croatia. In Croatia it began almost a year before it broke out in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And it -- but it's my understanding that it happened in similar way. The JNA moved in, the former JNA moved in, armed a considerable amount of people and then left the conflict and then also did that in places like Visegrad where the JNA came in for some time, disarmed the Muslim population, asked them to come back, and then left to the local Serbian detachments as well as members of the JNA that stayed there. You shake your head. Tell me why.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: That's your interpretation. My interpretation would be quite the opposite of yours. I think it would take a long time to explain it to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, and I guess -- yeah, I don't want to debate it with you, because I actually was -- it was just my impression of things, but I'm not here to dispute you. I'm referring to it an article called "Cooperation between the ex-JNA and the SDS terrorists," and it was in that journal of March 1993. Do you agree with the principles in that -- in that article?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: I don't remember any longer what that article says, but I know very well what that cooperation was like. The research we did and the documents we found explained with great precision and clarity how the cooperation between the JNA and the SDS took place, how the JNA participated in all this and held all the strategic moves in its hands and used very skillfully what they referred to as paramilitary units to achieve its strategic goals. In my deep conviction the JNA, on the basis of everything I've done so far, was a key player in all these events, and in fact the JNA pulled all the strings. The research we did on human losses and casualties, especially in Visegrad, indicate that murders of civilians took place in April when the JNA was in full control of Visegrad, and then in May -- on the 19th of May the JNA withdrew officially from Bosnia-Herzegovina but all its assets and the command staff and weapons stayed behind, and the crimes continued after the 19th of May and even intensified in June.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: That's kind of what I was surmising is that there was a considerable force of non-Bosnian Serb citizens that were sort of left behind and put in different uniforms, maybe with different insignias in the Visegrad theatre. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: In that period, April, May, and June, the dominant forces were the forces of the JNA. When we speak of the JNA, you must understand what the composition of that army was. Before Bosnia-Herzegovina was recognised as an independent state, it was a unified army in which people were organised. It was not a disorganised army. It had a strict chain of command and a strict control and command system, and it had full capacity to launch attacks and to kill, which is what it did, and also to hold under its control all those it wanted held under control, who acted outside the rules of that army. You're mentioning certain groups, so-called groups, but it's my position that there were no groups that were beyond the control of the JNA. They did not exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, and -- and that's -- I'm referring to a paragraph that: "In the case of the Vukovar open cooperation between the army and various Chetnik units, Seselj's men, Arkan's men, White Eagles, and other Serbian and Montenegrin and SDS units was neither hidden nor minimised." So it was early on that White Eagles and these paramilitary units were operating even in Vukovar. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: Yes. Those units acted openly and very aggressively both in Croatia and in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Evidently there was a strategy on the part of the JNA for the conflict in the region, especially in Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia, to be represented as a conflict between renegade units of the JNA and the legal forces of those two states. It was a very precisely prepared activity to distract the attention of the international community from the chief culprit, which was the JNA, and all in-depth investigations show that all the units you have just mentioned were under the command of the JNA. None of those units could have done anything at all had the generals of the JNA opposed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And going to another sentence that: "Just a small part of the army went, i.e., withdrew, mainly soldiers and officers, but most of them stayed under some other name and with different insignia together with the whole war technique, weapons, and including armoured units and air force." So is that true?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: From everything that was to happen, it was evident that only a small part withdrew, but the staff, the funding system, everything remained in place. I explained how they used so-called paramilitary formations to continue their activity in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Nothing actually changed. The hardware, the tanks, the weapons, it all stayed behind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Will you be concluding now, because we'll have to break.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honour, I literally have five tabs which probably would equal ten questions, but I think we should probably take the break and that's all I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Just a few more questions, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Just a few more questions and we can get you on your way. I'm still referring to the same article but kind of asking a little bit separate principle is, would it be fair to say that these paramilitary organisations such as the White Eagles travelled with the JNA into different areas that the JNA infiltrated?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: One could say that their name travelled. I'm not sure it was the same people travelling to the same places, but the name went round the region. Who the men were who were in those so-called paramilitary formations, it's very hard to establish.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, the reason I say that is there's been some testimony in this trial from the Muslims that were rounded up into the stadium in Visegrad and Colonel Jovanovic told them as a group that, "I control the White Eagles." And so it appears to me that right then and there the JNA acknowledged that the White Eagles were under their control, and I'm wondering if your commission had any information related to that.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: We had information. Some refugees arrived in Sarajevo and testified about those groups, but all that we could conclude from the information we had was that all those groups were more or less under the control of the JNA. It was our assessment that had they wanted to, they could have held those groups completely under control and prevented them from committing the crimes they committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And would it be true that in fact in Visegrad when the JNA left, they left the White Eagles there to wreak havoc on the population?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: I have already said when replying to your previous questions that the JNA withdrew only officially, only in formal terms, but in fact it did not withdraw. The commanders, the people under their command. For example, I remember a high ranking Colonel in Rudno [phoen] near Visegrad who was killed by some groups holding that area. The officer corps, the logistics support, everything stayed behind. Nothing changed in essence. Only the name changed. It was declared to be the army of Republika Srpska, whereas in fact it was just a branch of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, it's my understanding according to the article also that the JNA collaborated with the local SDS inner circles in each community to facilitate the arming of the Serbian population. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: You have a number of documents showing how weapons were distributed to the local Serbian population by the JNA. There are even lists with the types of weapons distributed at certain locations. This happened even before the beginning of the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: In fact, it began as early as 1991. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: Yes, in part. It began until late 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And has there -- have you undergone any investigation into these SDS inner circles that led each community as potential architects of the overall destruction of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: We're still doing that investigation. It's an ongoing process to explain the context and all the social and other circumstances in which the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina was prepared. This is ongoing research which will continue for many, many years. Some pieces of the puzzle are still missing. This Court is also working on this task. It's a long-term task.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Have you explored the war profiteers, the people that had very little before the war, Serbian ethnic origin, and now they have a lot, the company owners, hotel owners, property owners?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: We didn't focus on that problem because we were focusing on war crimes. The issue of war profiteers is something that the legal authorities in all the areas in the region, including Bosnia and Herzegovina, should deal with.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, further on in the bulletin there's an article about the victims of rape and how rape was an organised tool of the JNA to subjugate the females of the population. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: We produced a number of reports concerning rape. There's a book we worked on in 1999. In fact, we organised a large international conference in Sarajevo dedicated to the victimisation of women and we're still dealing with that problem. Not just rape but also other forms of sexual violence and other kinds of violence against women. Yes, we have dealt with that problem and will continue to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, and just looking at the article it appears that many, many municipalities had these sort of systematic rape scenario going on in them. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: That was something that happened in all parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina, especially the area we refer to as Podrinje. It's the area from Foca down the River Drina to Bijeljina, in Brcko, in Doboj, in Sarajevo. All other Bosnia-Herzegovina in various locations one can see that these things happened. We paid special attention to that, and, yes, one can conclude it was done systematically.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And systematically from the -- the Serbia and Montenegrin forces that had come into Bosnia left by the JNA. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: It's only partly so. Unfortunately, citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina also participated in these rapes. If you're asking about Visegrad, it did happen there, too, and it was done both by outsiders and, unfortunately, by local people as well, people from Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And just referring to the article, it states that: "Local Serbians did also take part although, although there are evidence that some Bosnian Serbs are forced into it, backed by the Serbian Montenegrin army." Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: Yes. I can give you a number of examples where there were even murders of Bosnian Serbs by the JNA because there were people forced to commit war crimes under very odd circumstances. I can give you an example from a project we're working on right now. We're trying to investigate that side of the war where citizens of one ethnic group helped those of another. For example, citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina of Serb ethnicity who assisted Bosniaks, Croats who helped the Serbs, and so on, Bosniaks who helped one or the other side. So we have a number of examples that show that war is not just black and white. There are examples of people who were courageous and who helped others. We found several such examples in Visegrad. Visegrad is not an isolated place. People did help each other, but unfortunately the crimes prevailed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And were there instances where one person might be forced to hurt one person but attempt to help another because they were torn but otherwise stuck in the war situation?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: I think there's a very interesting case. I think the man's last name is Pecikoza or something like that. We've just been investigating that case. I think he was some sort of SDS official at the time, if I recollect well, and he was playing a double role. In one role he was helping others, and in the other role he was doing evil things. It's a very confused story. He was evidently exposed to various kinds of pressure. We've been trying to explore the circumstances under which he was killed for helping citizens of other ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Because I've seen -- there's been testimony here where people saw him as a saviour of some people but then yet some other people had a totally different opinion of him. And it's Stanko Pecikoza, if I recall?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. You have contradictory information about one and the same person. That's quite possible, yes, because the circumstances were such that he played different roles, and what prevailed at any point in time, it's hard to say. The man is not alive, unfortunately. If he was, he might be able to tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, of course, you know, during this time there were other attacks besides rape. The religion was attacked and the mosques were destroyed. So there was also an attack on the Muslim population's entire faith, if you will. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: Well, you see, religious buildings were destroyed. Those are facts. Mosques in Visegrad were destroyed on someone's orders. The victims could see this as an attack on their religious affiliation. Of course one can view it like that, although I think personally that all this was used in order to escalate the level of violence and to get things to explode at a certain point in time. Religious and ethnic feelings were manipulated during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: So the architects of the whole process played on very personal and -- and religious things about the general population in order to force them to leave the area. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: Yes, I share that standpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But otherwise they really just wanted the land and to take it away and make sure these people moved away and didn't come back. Isn't that fair?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: Yes, more or less. The regime that instigated the conflict was a regime of fighting for power, a brutal power, using all possible methods to expand their power. The regime, and you know what regime that was. The man who was here unfortunately died before we could see the end of the trial, but he played on people's feelings in a strategic way. He wanted to portray this as an ethnic or religious war, and this predominated especially in Bosnia-Herzegovina, which was a multi-ethnic and multi-faith community where -- where causing this kind of fire could lead to very negative consequences.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Because the rank-and-file soldiers were generally simpler people. They didn't have a lot of knowledge of these grander schemes but really could only be manipulated on very simple levels of religion and nationalism. Would that be fair?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: Yes, more or less that's how it was. The courts judge according to the principle of individual responsibility, and that's something one has to respect. Of course everyone's individual responsibility has to be proved and an appropriate judgement handed down, but no individual acts outside the environment he lives in. The government, the authorities from whom he receives orders, this is a huge moral and ethnic question both in theory and in practice and has been for over 60 years after World War II. Is an individual just someone who implements the orders of others or is he a murderer? I think that people act in a certain social environment, and sometimes they can become the extended arm of the force of the government or the state even if they don't really wish to do the things they are doing. They do things they would never do in other circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Thank you. Just a couple more questions, actually. One of the sections is you have a section on witnesses where testimonials from victims of around Bosnia are there, and I notice in this particular journal there are two statements from Visegrad, one of -- and I believe both have already testified here in the Tribunal, from reading the statements in the journal. How did you collect these, and are you still in possession of these actual statements?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: Well, at the beginning of my testimony I explained that we had a very precise methodology of work with witnesses. Of course if circumstances allowed, the professional part of the team tried to contact directly people who were either victims themselves or who were eyewitnesses and could testify to certain events. Statements concerning rapes were always taken in such a way as to protect the identity of the victim while showing in public that this did happen, because we were trying to encourage the victims to speak out. I assume that these -- no, actually, I'm absolutely sure that those statements are still in our archives, and they are at the disposal of prosecutors, whether those of the ICTY or of the domestic courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And do you catalogue them by region such as Visegrad or Gorazde or other areas?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: The system of processing information is such that in professional terms a relational database is established with information on the victim, the location, the kind of event that happened, the kind of incident. So searching through certain locations, if that's your -- the terms of your search, you can reconstruct what happened in a certain area. You can reconstruct the geographical distribution of crimes in various towns, including Visegrad, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, were these statements taken by the MUP or were these taken by you separately? Were they police statements that you then archived, the police statement, or is there a police statement and also one to your association?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD TOKACA
utterances.text: The statements we took directly is something we used, and we also used statements taken by other institutions. The decision to establish the commission when it was made, all government bodies were told to cooperate with it, so that some material was delivered to us but some, we collected ourselves. We were independent, and even in the case of police reports and statements taken by the police we wanted to check those because the methods used by the police were quite different from our own. So we used this only as input. We didn't take it for granted anything that the police sent us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour, and I would like to introduce into evidence 1D10-2707, which is the March 1993 bulletin of the commission for gathering facts on war crimes for the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D53, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Friedman, any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: No redirect, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, that concludes your evidence. We thank you for giving it, and you may now leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The next witness, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next witness is not a protected witness so I'll say his name. It's Islam Kustura. Your Honour, over the break it was brought to my attention that we have fallen short of our disclosure obligations with respect to this witness.
