I have informed Mr. Cepic and Mr. Alarid over the break as soon as I learned the information and I want to make the Chamber aware of how we have fallen short. While we have provided all the statements that will we were aware of, including the ICTY statements, in a recent computer search of all of our documents in our document collection, some other documents were revealed and unfortunately we did not review them in the time that we should have and they are just being discovered today. So I want to bring them to the Court's attention. I think they are small, very short documents, and hopefully will not be too disruptive to the trial, but the first document is a one and a half page addendum to a statement that this -- that this witness gave in 2003 to Bosnian authorities. We have provided both the original and the English translation of that document. The next document is a document that we view is Rule 68. It's three and a half page witness statement of another witness that alleges that no mistreatment occurred in Uzamnica. We provided the original document and we hope to have a translation by the end of the day. The third document is a one and a half page witness statement of another witness stating that this particular witness was involved in the making of chemical weapons. It's obviously Rule 68 material and that has been disclosed today in the original language. We are hoping to secure a translation of that have by the end of the day. The fourth document is six lines listing this particular witness as an accused prisoner on -- it appears on the letterhead of Republika Srpska, Visegrad, I believe the Ministry of Interior. And the last document, Your Honour, is a one-page document. I don't believe it falls either under Rule 66 or Rule 68 but it is a statement that this witness gave to RS authorities with respect to other people regarding their activities in preparing explosive devices. So it has nothing to do with his testimony but it would be our practice or my practice to disclose that. So I apologise to Defence counsel and to the Court for -- for this omission. It's my hope that -- it's a total of seven pages, that if we are able to produce the translations to Defence counsel this evening that hopefully they feel that they -- tomorrow morning they'd be able to conclude their cross-examination. If not, if the Chamber believes fairness requires us to recall this witness for cross-examination at a later stage, we would of course endeavour to do that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, as much as the Chamber admires the frankness with which you confess these omissions, we have to say that they're happening all too frequently, and we must ask you to take care to see that disclosures are made in a timely manner as required by the Rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will review the procedures and make corrections, and again I do apologise to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Now, I want to deal, before the witness comes in, with the matter raised by Mr. Cepic, and Ms. Marcus is involved in that. Ms. Marcus, have you been brought up-to-date? What can you tell us about this second updated report which is said to have discrepancies?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: From the first.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Your Honours, we filed on the 9th of September a motion to substitute Dr. Tabeau's updated report for her old report. This was a few days after we received the updated report from Dr. Tabeau. In that motion we explained that none of Dr. Tabeau's overall conclusions have changed but that some numerical and statistical calculations had been updated. Your Honours, the nature of Dr. Tabeau's work is that it is based upon databases and sources which are constantly being updated and populated. For example, more bodies have been exhumed and identified today than one year ago and so on. Annex a to that September 9th motion contains a list outlining each and every change in the expert report for ease of reference and to facilitate the comparison exercise which the Defence and the Chamber may wish to undertake. Annex B was the updated expert report. Therefore the issue of the updated expert report is a matter which we were seeking to deal with in written pleadings. My understanding is that the Defence team for Milan Lukic filed a response, the deadline is today, but that the Defence team for Sredoje Lukic did not file a response. On this matter, Your Honours, in relation to Milan Lukic's assertion in -- in their response that the evidence of Dr. Tabeau is irrelevant and untimely, as the Trial Chamber has already determined that matter on the 23rd of July, 2008, that she qualifies as an expert and that her evidence is relevant and probative, I submit that this -- this submission by the Defence of Milan Lukic is untimely. And to my knowledge, the Defence did not file -- neither Defence team filed a motion for certification to appeal the decision of the 23rd of July and therefore I submit that any questions the Defence may have in relation to this can properly be put to Dr. Tabeau during cross-examination. Lastly, Your Honours, with respect to the charts which we have discussed numerous times, as I said in my submissions yesterday, it would take an inordinate amount of time for the Prosecution to ask Dr. Tabeau victim by victim to look into her databases, use her analytical expertise and tell us what her databases reflect in terms of these individuals' status as missing persons. Now, Dr. Tabeau's expert report contains an annex which is an excerpt of the ICRC missing persons database so that excerpt from the ICRC database is contained in Dr. Tabeau's report but the charts were meant to facilitate the presentation of that evidence to the Chamber and in the interests of efficiency and time saving. Therefore, Dr. Tabeau has access to these resources. She was able to provide those answers in the chart form which I submit was merely to facilitate the process. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How big is Annex A that sets out the discrepancies?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Just a moment, Your Honour. I will check exactly. Three pages and three lines. That's three sides of a page and plus an additional three lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, but on Monday morning, and my learned friend did confirm during the examination yesterday, we received new exhibit, completely now exhibits, and that is the main problem. We received the list which OTP expert filed, as I understood, during the weekend and during previous period with the new list which are completely different than the previous annexes with -- related to missing persons. And I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The annex that sets out the discrepancies is just three pages, though, three and a half pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have to check all those lists. I received yesterday more than couple hundred names on two list, which are completely different than the previous lists.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I submit there appears to be some confusion. The charts, again, which I'm calling charts so that we can differentiate it maybe from lists, one chart is the names of the victims as named in the indictment. The other chart is additional names. These charts were prepared, as I said, by Dr. Tabeau over the weekend in anticipation of her testimony as a demonstrative exhibit to facilitate asking her what her databases reflect in terms of the -- the reports of those people going missing. Now, we can use time in court and compare each name to the list, but that is exactly why I tried to find a method, and Dr. Tabeau came up with a method herself of presenting the results of that evidence and that was indeed done over the weekend. Your Honours, just -- we are perfectly happy -- as Mr. Groome said yesterday, we are perfectly happy, if need be, to continue with Dr. Tabeau now and if ever she needs to be called back for any reason, she is available at the convenience of the Chamber at any time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, with your leave. Just to add something. This is one of the main discrepancies. The base for the previous report was the Annex A which was the report from the Red Cross organisation about the missing persons. Now we had a list from indictment, and that caused many, many discrepancies between all the other discrepancies. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, we have to stop this now --

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- and I'll give a ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, the Chamber is not with you on this one. We don't see that you will suffer any -- any real prejudice. We expect you to cross-examine tomorrow, and should it be necessary to recall Dr. Tabeau, then as the Prosecution has indicated, she is available. Let the witness be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit. And you may begin, Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, can you hear me clearly?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: Yes. I can't hear.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Perhaps the court usher could help the witness in increasing the volume of the headphones. Mr. Witness, could you please state your full name.

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead. Kustura, Islam.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: What is your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Can you give us the precise date of your birth, please, the date and the month?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: The 15th of March.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: In which municipality were you born?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: In Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: What is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Before the war what work did you do?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: I was a farmer.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Are you married?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Do you have any children?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: I had seven, but two of my sons were killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Do you have any grandchildren?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: Yes, and grandchildren.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Kustura, how is your vision? Do you see well?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: No, not really.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Do you know what the diagnosis is, what is the reason for the poor vision?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: I have a cataract. That's what they say.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Is that affecting one eye or both eyes?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: Both.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Since when have you had these problems with your eyes?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: Since last autumn.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Kustura, do you recall where you were at the end of May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: 1992, in Visegrad, in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Before you were in the camp, months before that, do you recall where you were in May?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: I was at home. I was making sure everything was all right back home. I was at home, and I was hiding in the woods.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: What were you doing while you were hiding in the woods?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: We were running from the Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: How many men and women were with you in your hiding place in the woods?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: Seven or eight women and seven or eight men.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: How did you manage to protect yourselves?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: We made tents. We had tarpaulin that we used to make tents, so we hid there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Were any of your group armed?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: Yes. My son and a man named Ahmed. They were both killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, the name of your son.

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: Ibrahim Kustura.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And you mentioned a man named Ahmed. Can you tell us his family name, his surname?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: Mutapcic, Ahmed. He was a neighbour of ours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you left the woods and went back to your house?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: We spent the whole summer hiding in the woods until autumn. I think the 3rd of October, or 3rd of November. We were hiding in the woods. And then they caught us in the house.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes. I'd like to talk about that, when they caught you in the house, as you say. Who was it who caught you in the house?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: Vukasinovic, Nedjo Vukasinovic. And there was also Milko Bugarin. That's what they called him. He was a teacher. And there was another man who came by. He was walking down a road, and then I asked Nedjo and then he said that is a man from Bosanska Jagodina, yeah, him, too, but I can't remember the name.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Kustura, I'm going to interrupt you. We're going to come back to what you were just talking about, but I'd like to continue with -- with what happened before the incident you are now describing. There was an incident involving your son. He'd like to discuss that incident first. Can you tell us what happened to your son?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: My son came that morning, early that morning. My mother was at home, and she was preparing some food. They came to get their meals, and they were killed right there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Can you describe the incident during which your son was killed?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: Serb soldiers arrived in the village. They took us prisoners in the village right next to my house and marched us to a creek. They told the women to go to Dobrun and left the men there. So we were sitting there when a Serb soldier stood up and told Ahmed, "You follow me. I want to interrogate you." So Ahmed left, and then another man stood up and told my Ibrahim, "You, too, get up. I will interrogate you." And they took them as far as the creek and they were killed there. We heard rifle shots.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Kustura --

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: And later --

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Let's just take it step-by-step. Do you know who any of these Serb soldiers you're referring to? Do you know any of their names?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: I do. Dragan Savic, who is the man who took my Ibro away. I don't know the others. It was all mixed up.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: How do you know that Dragan Savic was the one who took your Ibro away?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: I know, because I had been in the camp at Visegrad, and then at one point a soldier came and said, "Kustura, Dragan Savic wants to see you." So I went there, and he beat me and he said, "Tell us who killed your son. Tell us who killed your son." I wasn't able to admit -- I didn't admit this to anyone, but I do know that later that evening when we left, when the guard took me along, he said, "Dragan Savic, fuck him, came here to look for something," or rather vaguer.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Kustura, did you see your son actually being killed?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: No. It was over near the creek. How could I possibly see?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Did you see his body after he was killed?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: Yes, we did, later when Salko, my neighbour and I, came running, we saw the soldiers and both the bodies were in the creek, and you could see body of Ibrahim. It wasn't entirely submerged. The head was still above the surface. And then after eight or ten days, and we hadn't been allowed to bury the bodies, so before daybreak one day we went there. We got the bodies, and we gave the bodies a burial.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Do you recall the date on which your son was killed?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Earlier you mentioned that you were captured on the 3rd of October or the 3rd of November. You said you weren't sure of the date. Was your son killed before that or after that?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: The 3rd. Before. Before.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to take you back to what you started to tell us about before I interrupted you to speak about your son. You told us that you were caught in your house, and you said you think it was the 3rd of October or the 3rd of November, and you mentioned some names of some individuals who came to that house. I'd like to return to that. Could you tell us what those people who came to your house -- what they said to you?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: Dragan Pejovic was there. He was the one guarding my son. Dragan Pejovic, a neighbour of mine from the area. And they kept saying, "Don't be afraid. Don't be afraid." But then they got as far as the creek, and what happened there was something entirely different.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, let's go back to the 3rd of October or the 3rd of November, as you said earlier.

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: The 3rd of October, I think that was.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what happened on that day?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: What happened. They killed them. We fled to the woods, and we were hiding in the woods with a tarp and the tents. There were women there and men too.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Kustura, a little bit earlier you mentioned a name. The name you mentioned was Vukasinovic, Nedjo Vukasinovic.

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: Nedjo Vukasinovic used to be a good friend of mine before the war, and maybe he was the one who helped save us.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: You told us that he, among others, caught you in the house.

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: Caught us, yes. Yes, that's right. It was him. He caught us. He said, "Don't be afraid. Don't be afraid. We won't harm you." And then Nedjo gave me a pack of cigarettes. I lit up. And Salko got some cigarettes too. And then we left for Visegrad. He drove us in a car to Visegrad, and then they went to the command to report, for Nedjo to report.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: When you say "command," can you tell us where precisely they took you?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: This was the school in Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Can you tell us the name of the school?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: Hasan Veletovac. I think that's what it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And where were you taken from the school?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: We didn't even go inside the school. We stayed by the car. The police arrived and said, "Get back in the car. You're going back home this evening." And they drove us straight to Uzamnica, to the camp there. We found some children there in the camp. We thought at first they were Serbian children, but in fact they were Muslim children. There was a woman who had been taken prisoner with two children.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Kustura, you mentioned before you got to Uzamnica that you encountered some police who told you to get into the car. Do you know any of these police officers by name?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: No, I don't know them.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: How do you know that they were police?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: By their uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Can you tell us the colour of the uniforms?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: Blue.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned Uzamnica. Can you tell us what Uzamnica was? What kind of a location was this?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: It was a barracks, and there were military depots there, 27 hangars with ammunition, but all that was taken off to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: How many barracks were there at Uzamnica?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: Only one.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Where were your wife and mother taken?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: That evening when it got dark they separated us off. The men went to one hangar and the women to another. There were some other men there in the hangar, but we didn't see them. They just shoved me inside, and afterwards I got to know the men inside.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Kustura, were you in regular contact with your wife and mother?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: No. No. I didn't see them for eight or ten days at a time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Were you free to move about?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: No, God forbid.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Why not? What was it which prevented you from moving about?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: About? The Chetniks wouldn't let us. The door was always closed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours, could we go, please, into private session for the next few questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Kustura, can you describe the conditions in Uzamnica?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: You know what it was like? We lay down on the concrete floor. We got up from the concrete floor. If we had any clothes with us, we put them on. If we didn't, we didn't. It was all just concrete.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: What was the food like?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: It was terrible. They would bring us just a little bowl of soup for two of us to share.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: What were the bathroom facilities like?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: We didn't have any at all. There were two black buckets. We used one to pass water and the other one to bring water for us to wash in.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Was there heat in the winter?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: God forbid. Throughout the winter someone would bring some paper, and then the next day the soldier would come and swear at him right away.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Was the room you were staying in, the hangar, was it closed or open to the air?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: It was closed. There was an iron door.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Who were the guards at Uzamnica? Did you know any of them?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: There was Mico Spasojevic. He was the guard. But there were others, lots of others. I used to know their names, but I've forgotten now.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Were there always the same guards?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: Yes, always the same ones except that two were sent off to the front line. What was his name? He beat me up once.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Do you recall how many guards --

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: I think it was Ilija Sestric.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Do you recall how many guards you saw?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: There were seven or eight sometimes and just two or three at other times.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Who was the commander of the guards?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: Mico Spasojevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Do you know if he was the commander of all of Uzamnica?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: No. No, just of the guards. Just the guards.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Did you ever suffer any direct mistreatment at the hands of the guards?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: Mico Spasojevic hit us on two occasions. He did. The others didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And how did he beat you on those occasions?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: You know how? He made himself a kind of whip, and then he tied a piece of iron to the end, a piece of lead and he beat us with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Did you ever suffer any mistreatment at the hands of others apart from the guards?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: Only Milan Lukic and Sredoje, and they would bring company.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Please describe to us the first time you saw Milan Lukic.

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: I saw him several days after my arrival. He came right away.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: How do you know that this was Milan Lukic?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: They told me. I didn't know him, but they told me, the others.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Did you know Milan Lukic from before?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: I didn't know him, but I did know Sredoje.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: How did you know Sredoje from before?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: He was in the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: The first time you saw Milan Lukic in Uzamnica, what did he do?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: You know what he did? All the worst. He hit us, beat us. He did all sorts of things.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: With what did he beat you?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: First he would run at us like the priest's horse and kick us. He kicked us all, and then people fell over, and then afterwards he would use whatever he wanted, a rifle, his fists, his -- he would kick us. He used everything.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Did you hear him say anything while he was beating you?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: He didn't say why he was beating us. He would just say, "Hit the balija."

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Was anyone else present during this first time you were beaten?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: He beat everyone, all of us in turn, and he didn't stop until he'd beaten up everybody.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Was there anybody with Milan Lukic during this incident?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: Sredoje was with him always.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Did Sredoje --

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: Sometimes there would be three or four carloads coming to Uzamnica and they would beat us as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: With regards to Sredoje, did Sredoje do anything to you?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: Yes, together with Milan, everything.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: As a result of that beating did you suffer any injuries?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: Of course I did. When I arrived in Sarajevo, I was all black and blue. My arms were broken. My chest, my back were all black. When I got to Sarajevo an ambulance arrived, and they said I should be X-rayed, and when they X-rayed me I had things on my ribs, on my back, everywhere like bulges. And then there was a man called Prepajac [phoen]. He took the X-rays. And there was a lady doctor and I said, "what's this on my back," and she said, "Grandfather, you were beaten up a long time ago. I don't know what happened to you," and I said -- or, rather, she thought I had fallen down and hurt myself and I said, "no, it's the Chetniks who beat me up," and then Ahmet arrived and I --

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You asked him what Sredoje did, but he didn't really tell you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes. I'm going back to that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Kustura, I asked you before, as His Honour has said, what did Sredoje do, and you said, "Yes, together with Milan, everything."

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: He beat me just as Milan did.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Can you describe specifically what Sredoje did to you?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: Well, he hit me just like Milan did.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: What did he use to hit you?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: First he kicked me, and then later with a rifle, and then they would bring stakes, stakes and hit us with those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Made of what? What were the stakes made of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How big were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A metre and a half or two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Kustura, after the first beating what condition were you in at that time? Rather than describing later in Sarajevo, at that time, after the first beating that you described, what was your physical condition?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: Terrible. I was all broken, all beaten up. I was in a terrible state.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Were you able to move around after that first beating?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: No, I wasn't, no. And after the second one I had to lie down for 18 days.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Tell it us about the second one. What are you referring to the second time?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: You know what? They broke me. They smashed me. I couldn't move. I laid down on that concrete for 18 days.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Who was it who caused you the injuries which resulted in you being immobile for 18 days?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: Milan.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Can you describe to us the incident?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: Of course I can describe it. They beat you for as long as they hear that you're breathing.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: When you say "they," could you tell us specifically who it was who beat you?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: You just said, "They beat you for as long as they hear that you're breathing." Could you tell us who "they" is? Who did this?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: Milan and Sredoje, and sometimes they would bring companions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: How often would you say you saw Milan Lukic in Uzamnica?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: I saw him all the time until he went off to get a shop at Kalemegdan, and when he came back from Belgrade he said, "Will you give it to me," and this man said, "I will, Milan, just don't beat me any more." And Milan went to Kalemegdan. That Serb didn't give him the shop, and Milan took a pistol and killed the Serb and he lay there in Belgrade five or six months [Realtime transcript omitted "five or six months"], maybe, and we were in Dobrun and his sister welcomed Milan Lukic from Belgrade from prison. That's how it was and we got all excited what would happen now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Just want to intervene in transcript. I think we haven't got translated how long Milan remained in custody in Belgrade, and I think that the witness answered on that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know it. Might have been four or five months that he stayed there in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Perhaps this is a matter for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, it would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's a matter of the transcript, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: As my learned friend added, it is a matter of transcript because this witness mentioned it in his examination but interpreters couldn't catch that part, so thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Can I continue, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let me be clear, Mr. Cepic. What do you say the transcript is missing something?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: How long a witness said that Milan Lukic remained in Belgrade prison for five months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: We can listen to tape. And my intervention was this is not the part in transcript. It's not recorded in transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's not in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't talk about that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: We can check, listening by the tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: May I ask the interpreters whether the witness --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the interpreters find it very difficult to understand the witness, and there are some parts which the interpreter did not hear properly or understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll proceed. If you wish to make an issue of it in cross-examination you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Okay, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just to put out any blame on me, you know, and any doubt, because I'm so confident that I heard that. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not questioning your integrity at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Kustura, how often did Milan Lukic mistreat you?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: Well, if it wasn't every day it was every other day, and he would bring two or three cars with people and Sredoje, and they would beat people.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: How often would you say Sredoje would beat you?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: Well, the same as Milan. The same.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Did you ever see Milan Lukic come alone to Uzamnica?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: No, he never came alone.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Do you recall what Milan Lukic was wearing usually when he came to Uzamnica?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: A military uniform. That's what he wore.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Do you recall what Sredoje Lukic was wearing when he came to Uzamnica?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: Both of them, both of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Did you ever see either of them dressed any differently?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: No, I never did. Only military uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Was Milan Lukic usually carrying anything when he came to Uzamnica?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: What?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Was Milan Lukic carrying anything in his hands when he came to Uzamnica?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: Once he brought a stake. I'm mentioning the stake again. And he beat us with that stake.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Apart from the stake, did they carry any other weapons?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: Yes. They always came with weapons. He wouldn't go around without weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Did you see Sredoje Lukic carrying anything when he came to Uzamnica?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: No, I didn't. Just his hands and his submachine-gun which he carried.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Kustura, how long were you detained in Uzamnica?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: Three years and ten days.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Can you describe the interaction between Milan Lukic and the Uzamnica guards?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: Milan, when he came, if the door was closed, if the guard had closed the door and gone off somewhere, Milan would open the lock and by the time the guard came back he would have beaten us all.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Could we go into private session for the next few questions, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: "Come on, (redacted) he said, "Let's go there and see if (redacted) is still alive," and then we went there and (redacted) was still slightly alive so we pulled him out of the puddle and carried him back into the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Can you tell us -- you've used two names. One is (redacted) The other is (redacted) Is that the same person?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: Yes, yes. The same person. He is short. That's why we called him (redacted) which is diminutive.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Kustura, during your detention did you ever directly see any prisoners being taken out by Milan Lukic?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: I saw him hundreds of times beat us, all of us. He was a tall man. He would come to the door and then he would kick someone and people fell down and he would go on beating them.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Did you ever witness Milan Lukic take anyone away who never returned again?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Objection, leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Agreed. Don't answer the question. You have to reformulate it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Kustura, did you ever see with your own eyes Milan Lukic take anybody away?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Same objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I allow that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nermin and the man from Rogatica. I saw him take them away.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Who took them away?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: Milan and Sredoje.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Did you ever witness any killings during the time you were in Uzamnica?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You can ask him whether he saw -- he ever saw them again, they having been taken away. That's not objectionable.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, they never returned.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Kustura, what happened to your mother?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: She died in the camp because of all the suffering. She just died. There you go. She had to watch what they were doing to us. She had to listen to all the stories about the hangar and everything. She just had to die. She had no choice.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Were you able to bury her?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: Other camp inmates went and buried her body somewhere. I still don't know where it was that they buried her, nor do I have anyone to ask. It was all blown apart, no inmates remaining, and I simply have no way of knowing where she was buried.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: What happened to your wife?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: My wife died in Sarajevo after we had left the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Were you ever given any medical treatment for any of the injuries you suffered as a result of the beatings?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, always. They would always take me. My daughters-in-law would take me to see a doctor that was at the hospital nearby and my daughter-in-law took me there, and that's where I received treatment.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Kustura, during the time that you were imprisoned in Uzamnica, were you given any medical care?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: Perish the thought. Never. Who could possibly give me medical care, perhaps the same people who were beating me up and killing me. Do you think they would have given me any medical care?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Did the Red Cross ever visit Uzamnica?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: Five times, six perhaps. They came, but the Serbs never allowed them to enter the camp. The one time they did they said they were telling the Red Cross that we were just having a Sunday walkabout, that nobody had to do anything at all. There were two military toilets there, and they said, "This is the one that they use," but actually we were using buckets and not those facilities.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: How did you ultimately manage to get out of the detention centre?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: There was an exchange, all for all. They released Serbs. They released Muslims. Depending on where you were from. They sent us to Sarajevo, and the Serbs probably to their own areas.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Was your wife released with you?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: She was, yes. At the same time. There were other women there, too. They were all released.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Do you recall the date of your release?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: The 10th of December.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Do you recall what year that was?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: 1994, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Marcus. Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Kustura.

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Do you recall giving statements before in this case, and do you recall giving a statement in November of 1994?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: Yes. I've lost track. I can't remember all of them, can I?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, and the reason I say that is you just testified you got out of the prison in December 1994, and it seems that you gave the statement a month before that. So I'm clarifying that. And so maybe the better question is, isn't it true you got out of Uzamnica October of 1994 instead of December?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: Might be. That just might be. I forget.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And before October of 1994, when was the last time you believe you saw Milan Lukic?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: Well, we didn't see him for quite a long time because he was over in Belgrade in the prison, so we didn't see him. Then they said he'd come back as soon as he was back from that prison, and then once he came back with the guards' commander, and he said, "Is there anything you need, coffee, brandy, sugar? Milan is your man. I'll bring you everything." And nobody dared speak a word. And I was just standing there and I said, "Milan, bring us all you can. We need everything." So he left and he never returned. And we were exchanged soon, fortunately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Dieckmann.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, just for clarification, my learned friend Mr. Alarid did not mention that he's the counsel for Mr. Milan Lukic, just for clarification for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, that's noted.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And you indicate that he came there sometime before you were released in the exchange. Can you tell us how long before?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: Ten days, eight or ten days.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And before that, when was the last time you had seen --

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: The last time was then, when he came to the hangar to ask if we needed anything so he could bring it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And on that occasion is it fair that he did not hurt anybody that you saw?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: No, no. No, he didn't, not then. He was as meek as a lamb that time he came. We just stood up, as we always did, lined up, and he said, "Sit down. Sit down. Stay where you are." That's how it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And before that time you indicated that you -- before that time you indicated that you believed he was in prison in Belgrade, and so how much further earlier had you seen him last?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: I didn't see him again after he'd left and went to that prison in Belgrade. I never saw him again after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And when do you believe he went to that prison in Belgrade, if you can tell us?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: There was that man who had owned two shops at Kalemegdan and there were Serbs working there, so Milan went there and asked that man, "Will you give me those shops," and he said, "I will, Milan, just don't hit me. Just take them, and that's that." And then Milan went the other time and killed this Serb at Kalemegdan, and then they locked him up. Locked him behind bars.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: What's more important to me, sir, and it's only if you can remember, is do you remember the month and the year that you believe that that happened?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: It was the summer, the last summer when we left the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And so you're saying it's the summer of 1994?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And so you're saying that you saw him at the camp between when you got there, every other day until the summer of 1994?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Could you please describe this Milan Lukic.

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: Tall man, clean-shaven, tall.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Hair colour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How tall. How tall, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 190, 180, 190, tall.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: What was his hair colour?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: Sorry? I didn't get that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: What colour was his hair?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: How long his hair was. Always closely cropped. He never had long hair.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: What colour?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Did you know the colour of his eyes?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: That, I don't know. I swear. I never looked him in the eye. There was no time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: How old are you today, sir?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: I was born in 1930, so you can do the math for yourself. The 15th of March, that's my birthday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And after your arrival at the barracks, what was the first time you believe you saw Milan Lukic?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: The second or third day. He came right away.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And you were there in October of 1992? Is that true?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: Yes, the 3rd of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And did you talk to all the inmates that were in your side of the barracks, the men's side?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: Yes. Well, later on in the evening you would do some whispering and just talk and lie down.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, when you were brought there you were brought by a police car; correct?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And you were brought there by policemen in police uniforms; correct?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And do you know if the other inmates were also brought there by police cars?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: No, I don't know. I don't know. I didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Were you ever taken -- during your arrest were you ever taken to the SJB in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: No. They first took us to the school and from the school straight to Uzamnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Do you know Hajrudin Mutapcic?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: If he gave a statement indicating that he could stay at your house and you used to be involved in making explosives, would that be true?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: One microphone at a time, please, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's not Hajrudin Mutapcic. That's a different name.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Were you ever involved in making explosives during the resistance?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: No, not me. [Microphone not activated] saw neighbours do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Could you repeat that, please, sir?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: I saw them make explosives at my neighbour's place. They would put it all together and then wrap it up in order to throw it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters can't hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Would you please repeat what you just said, Witness? The interpreter didn't hear.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the all the other microphones please be switched off. We can't hear on account of all the background noise. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't make explosives myself, not ever, but I did see other people do things.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Did you know the names of these neighbours that made explosives?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: Halid's son, Halid Kahriman. They did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: When your arm was broken, I think you stated that you never got any medical attention. How did you set the breaks?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: Well, it just stopped by itself and that was that. I was all black and blue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But you indicate in your statement that after a beating, both arms were broken, one in three places and the other one in one place, and I'm wondering how you could recover from that.

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: Well, I had no choice but to recover, did I. There was no medical assistance. I don't know exactly how it occurred, but it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Is it possible that your arms were not broken but you just thought they were because of the pain?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: There certainly was a great amount of pain. And it's not that I thought they were broken. I'm absolutely certain they were broken.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But your arms were -- how long until you were able to use your arms again to do anything?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: Six months, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Do you remember in what month and what year your arms were broken?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: I don't know, I swear. The first or the second year.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: If you were brought in in October of 1992, how many months after your initial being brought in?

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: Could have been sometime midway through the winter.

utterances.speaker: ISLAM KUSTURA
utterances.text: It could have been 1993 or it could have been 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Alarid. Mr. Cepic, or is it Mr. Dieckmann?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Dieckmann has been preparing for cross-examination for this witness but we kindly ask if we can start tomorrow morning because we've been waiting for translation for these additional statements that Mr. Dermot Groome mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, would you just remind me of these statements?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That was our shortcoming in the disclosure that I mentioned before the witness testified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Oh, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the further information about it is that those translated pages will be available hopefully sometime tomorrow midmorning.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If we adjourn now, then, tomorrow morning with whom would we start if this is not going to be available until midmorning?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I suggest we start with the cross-examination of Ewa Tabeau, and then when that's completed then the translation should be available. We'll get them to Defence counsel. Again it's just six pages, I believe, and we'll get them to Defence counsel as soon as they become available. Hopefully we could do the cross-examination then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll follow the procedure suggested by the Prosecutor. Tomorrow morning, then, at ten minutes to 9.00. 8.50 a.m. Witness, we are going to adjourn now. We're going to adjourn now, so you can leave when we leave, and you'll be told when to return tomorrow. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, all right. At what time should I come here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We have persons --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We have persons within the Tribunal who will tell you that. They will tell you when to return. It's likely to be sometime in the middle of the morning, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 24th day of September, 2008, at 8.50 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: [Private session]  [Confidentiality partially lifted by order of Chamber]
--- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.44 p.m.,
